newsitem.title: USA: Nine million new U.S. voters, but boredom may rule.
newsitem.headline: Nine million new U.S. voters, but boredom may rule.

text.p: Some nine million more Americans have registered to vote since the 1994 congressional elections but history and a lackluster contest suggest many will not bother to cast a ballot on Nov. 5.

The United States has the second-worst record for voter turnout among 20 democracies studied by the League of Women Voters, leading only Switzerland, and League President Becky Cain says 1996 has many signs of another low-turnout year.
"In this country, we tell you you have a constitutional right to vote, but ... we made it extremely complicated to exercise it," Cain said in a telephone interview.
Compared to other democracies, Cain said, registration is difficult in the United States and there is no law to compel voting, as there is in Belgium, Australia and Italy.

The League's statistics show that only 53 percent of registered voters went to the polls on average in the 1980s, compared with 94 percent in top-ranked Belgium, 79 percent in middle-of-the-pack Israel and 49 percent in Switzerland.

But that was before passage of the National Voter Registration Act, known as "the Motor Voter Law" because it lets people register when they get their driver's licenses as well as other convenient means, including by mail.

It took effect in January 1995. A study by the League found that 9 million new voters had registered by June 1996 and estimated that as many as 15 million new voters will have been registered by Election Day.
If there is voter malaise, Cain blamed it on opinion polling and news reporting that suggest this election has already been decided in favour of President Bill Clinton, over Republican Bob Dole.
"It is very frustrating in many ways for us to have the election declared over before we as citizens have had an opportunity to participate," Cain said.

She said the Motor Voter Law could lay the foundation for future higher turnout with a more diverse and representative electorate. Although Republicans feared the new law would cut into their rolls, Cain said Republican registrations remained stable while Democratic registrations fell about one percent.
Americans increasingly decline to list an official party affiliation and most areas no longer require it in any case.
John Zogby, a pollster who does surveys for Reuters among others, also sees potential for a rock-bottom turnout.

"We still have double-digit levels of undecided voters," Zogby said by telephone, noting that just two weeks before the ballot the level of undecided voters is in the double digits. "Presumably at least a chunk of those undecideds won't vote," he said.
At this stage in 1992, undecided voters accounted for only 8 or 9 percent of those polled, Zogby said.

There have been a number of voter registration drives aimed at young people such as "Rock the Vote" and "Choose or Lose." Other efforts have targeted African-Americans, Asian-Americans, Latinos, Chinese-Americans and the disabled.
The total number of registered voters in the United States is elusive, with the New York-based research group Human SERVE estimating it at more than 131 million.

Another group, the Committee for the Study of the American Electorate, refuses to make an estimate but says only about 70 percent of those eligible to vote -- basically, American citizens aged 18 and older -- will be registered.
